body.heading: Nine coins, one secret
paragraphs: Nine coins sit in a row, identical to the eye. One of them is slightly heavier than the rest. You have a balance scale — the old-fashioned kind with two pans — and you may use it exactly twice. No guessing: your method must guarantee finding the heavy coin.

Weighing coins one against one would take far too many tries. The breakthrough is realising that a balance gives you three outcomes, not two: left side down, right side down, or perfectly level. Every weighing can sort coins into three stories at once.

body.heading: Think in threes
paragraphs: Split the nine coins into three groups of three. Weigh group A against group B. If A sinks, the heavy coin is in A. If B sinks, it is in B. If the pans balance, it must be in group C, the group you left off the scale. One weighing, and nine suspects have become three.

Now repeat the trick inside the guilty group: weigh one coin against another. If one side sinks, that coin is the heavy one. If they balance, the third coin — the one still in your hand — is the heavy one. Two weighings, case closed.

body.heading: Why two weighings are enough
paragraphs: Each weighing has three possible outcomes, so two weighings can tell apart 3 × 3 = 9 situations — exactly the nine coins that might be heavy. The maths and the method fit each other perfectly.

That is also why the trick extends: three weighings could find one heavy coin among 27. If you enjoy this, set the puzzle for a friend with nine identical-looking coins or bottle caps and one secretly marked underneath — and watch them discover the power of three.

takeaway: Split into threes, weigh, and let the scale point at the guilty group — two weighings, nine suspects, one heavy coin.
